The plaintiff is a disabled son of the donor and for such reason he has been given the suit property by way of gift. He then referred section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act that it is also a mode of transfer and it is by way of gift and if it relates to immovable property it is to be registered. In this particular case, delivery of possession was made but no doubt it is to be registered as the property is immovable property. He submits that gift as per section 123 of Transfer of Property Act can be effected by delivery of possession. Even if it is not registered but there is delivery of possession therefore, it a valid gift and that can be cured by subsequent registration by representative as the donor expired. The Court below without considering all those aspects and without going through the Exhibits while the donor himself by giving deposition before the Court that it has already been accepted by the plaintiff and he is in possession. Khatian marked as Exhibit 9 is the proof of possession of the appellant. Under these facts and circumstances the trial Court should have decreed the suit and such dismissal is required to be set aside. He further by referring Exhibit. A order sheet in Case No. 1/78-79 and the investigation report as submitted was not proved by any witnesses for the defendants, therefore, such report cannot be accepted and the report itself states that the property is to be seized and be included in Khatian No. 1. Therefore, it shows that the plaintiff-appellant is still in possession in the property. Under such circumstances, the appeal should be allowed in favour of the plaintiff-appellant. 

 7. Mr. AS Md. Ramzan Khan, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 submits that the plaintiff is the owner by dint of a gift made by his father which is not at all a gift under law. He then by referring the Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order, 1972 that a person cannot hold land more than 100 bights and it is barred by article 5A of the said Order the excess land will be seized and will be in khatian No.1. Further, by referring section 123 of Transfer of Property Act that the transfer by way of gift must be registered. Section 129 says that section 123 shall not affect any Rule of Muslim Law. He then submits that Article 358 sub-Article 2 of Hindu Law says that any gift made there under will be effected in the manner stipulated under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act and further submits that for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument. Therefore, the gift as that has been referred as per Exhibit 1 is not at all a gift in the eye of law. Further he submits by referring 35 DLR (AD) 31 that if a person make a gift of immovable property other than Muslim it must be registered. According to Muslim Law, gift of movable and immovable property made by a Muslim will be valid even if it is not registered but delivery of possession must be there. Therefore, he submits that the basis of that gift made on a simple white paper by a Hindu not even registered is not a gift in the eye of law. The plaintiff cannot be entitled to claim that he is the owner of the property rather no witnesses categorically stated that he lives separately. This deed has actually been created for the purpose of avoiding section 5A of Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order, 1972 therefore, the Court below did not commit any wrong in dismissing the suit. 

 11. Further, it appears that the property has been seized and possession was taken up and it has been included in Khatian No. 1. PW 4 in his cross-examination, stated that from the office record it is seen that possession of the suit land was taken over by the Government. The CO(Rev) forfeited the suit land vide order No. 6 dated 28-3-79. The decision cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the deed even if not registered that can be cured on registration by the representative. But law says that it must be registered as per section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act signed by the donor and attested by witnesses. Therefore, the deed of gift does not stand at all and even if that gift as accepted that has been done after promulgation of Article 5A of the Bangladesh Land Holding (Limitation) Order, 1972. Under such circumstances there is no merit in the appeal.
